newsitem.title: UK: UK's new Chancellor preaches financial prudence.
newsitem.headline: UK's new Chancellor preaches financial prudence.

text.p: It is somehow fitting that Gordon Brown, Britain's newly appointed Chancellor of the Exchequer, is the son of a Church of Scotland minister.
It is Brown's job, as Labour's economics spokesman, to warn constantly of the eternal electoral damnation that will engulf the party if it strays from the virtuous path of sound finance.

And after four general elections at which Labour has been crucified for its loose talk on tax and spending, it is a task that Brown is likely to discharge with a Scottish preacher's dour intensity after the party's historic landslide in Thursday's election.

"Let me just reiterate, so no one misunderstands... Labour will not take risks with inflation and we reject old quick-fix solutions of tax, spend and borrow," he said in 1994 in a key-note statement which he has stuck to every since.
Colleagues in Labour's cabinet-in-waiting who have had even vague spending commitments ruthlessly redlined from speeches are the first to be left in no doubt that Brown means what he says.
Tax policy is similarly crafted to minimise Labour's exposure to attacks from the Conservatives and make sure Labour will balance the books in power.

Brown has committed Labour to lowering VAT on domestic fuel and levying a windfall tax on the profits of privatised utilities and the party has pledged to leave key income tax rates unchanged in the new parliament.

But Brown, 46, is unrepentant in his prudence. In rejecting a spending splurge as the solution to the pent-up demands of 18 years in opposition, he reasons that the world has changed and left-of-centre parties must change with it.

"Of course, a Labour government would want to do more for our frontline caring services and investment for the future. But we can only do so if we either reallocate resources... or by raising the growth rate," he has said.
In an age of global production and footloose capital, Brown recognises the economic role of the state has had to change.

In place of subsidies, nationalisation and state interference, government's task is to promote education, constant training for new skills and investment in technology so that British workers can outperform lower-wage economies.

"Past Labour tried to counter the injustice and failings of free market forces by substituting government for market... But the fact is that these policies cannot work in the highly integrated world economic environment in which we live." This leads Brown to stress the equality of opportunity -- giving people the education needed to do well -- in a break with the old Socialist creed of achieving equality of outcome by tinkering with redistributive taxes and welfare benefits.
Brown certainly looks the part of prudence and rectitude.
Doleful and brooding, he looks as though he could be trusted with the church's collection plate.

A football fanatic with a mordant wit that can electrify the House of Commons, Brown nevertheless cuts a somewhat lonely figure and sullen figure. One Labour insider said Brown is "in a state of disgruntled perpetual motion like some snorting bull". Driven and committed and are the words most used to describe Brown. A monumentally self-disciplined workaholic, he is an intellectual heavyweight who is never happier than when surrounded by his books.
Born in Glasgow on February 20, 1951, Brown took a first-class history degree at Edinburgh University before he was 20 and went on to complete a doctorate.
He was a lecturer, journalist and television editor before entering parliament as MP for Dunfermline East in 1983.

By 1987 he had already reached the equivalent of cabinet rank as "shadow" chief secretary for the treasury and then spent three years as Labour's industry spokesman before becoming shadow chancellor in 1992.
Instinctively pro-European, Brown sticks to Labour's official agnostic line on membership of a single currency while stressing the downside for Britain if it stays outside.
But he was forced to bow to the inevitable in November and announce that Labour would not take Britain into monetary union during its first five-year term without holding a referendum.

Brown and Tony Blair became close political allies as they rose rapidly through Labour's ranks. Both are on the modernising wing of the party, and it was an agonising decision for Brown to stand aside to give his friend a clear run for the leadership when former leader John Smith died in May 1994.

Writing in New Statesman magazine in May 1996, John Lloyd said Brown's solitary image, contrasting with Blair's well-advertised conventional family life, was a factor for those in the party who weighed up the two for future leader.

Brown had a five-year affair with Princess Marguerite, the eldest daughter of ex-King Michael of Romania, but memorably had to endure prying questions on BBC radio about why, in his mid-40s, he was still not married.
Too proud to flaunt heterosexuality for the press, Brown's response was more or less "mind your own business", Lloyd said.
"He is right to insist on the separation of the public and the private, but it is an increasingly besiged position.

"He may one day be a great politician. Or he may fail badly, at least by his own lights. He has already positioned himself so that he must make the attempt. It is a lonely place, even for a solitary man," Lloyd concluded.
